title: Gross National Product and Gross Domestic Product
path: Nigeria Economy and Health Care Delivery

headings.title: Introduction to Health Economics and Macroeconomic Indicators
headings.content: Health economics looks at how society allocates scarce resources for health and healthcare. While clinical nursing focuses on individual patient outcomes, macroeconomics looks at the entire country. Macroeconomic indicators provide a numerical snapshot of a nation's economic health. Policymakers use these statistics to decide how much money goes into public services, including the national health system. Nurses need a basic grasp of these numbers because economic downturns directly affect hospital budgets, drug supplies, and staffing levels.

headings.title: Defining Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
headings.content: Gross Domestic Product measures the total monetary value of all finished goods and services produced within a country's borders during a specific time period. Location is the key rule for GDP. If a service happens on Nigerian soil, it counts toward Nigeria's GDP, regardless of whether a Nigerian citizen or a foreign expatriate provided it. In healthcare, this includes every consultation, laboratory test, and surgical procedure performed inside hospitals located within the country.

headings.title: Defining Gross National Product (GNP)
headings.content: Gross National Product measures the total value of all finished goods and services produced by the permanent residents and businesses of a nation, no matter where they are physically located in the world. Ownership is the key rule for GNP. If a Nigerian-owned pharmaceutical company runs a factory in another country, the profits from that factory count toward Nigeria's GNP. Conversely, any economic activity by foreign nationals inside Nigeria is subtracted from GNP because those earnings belong outside the home country.

headings.title: Key Differences: Location versus Ownership
headings.content: The fundamental difference between GDP and GNP lies in their perspective on production. GDP is geographic, asking: 'Was this made inside our country?' GNP is nationality-based, asking: 'Was this made by our people or companies?' For developing nations with significant foreign investment in sectors like oil, telecommunications, and private healthcare, GDP is often higher than GNP because many profits leave the country to pay foreign owners.

headings.title: Application of Economic Metrics to Healthcare
headings.content: Governments track healthcare spending as a percentage of GDP to see how much national wealth goes toward medical care. When GDP grows, governments usually have more tax revenue to build clinics, buy vaccines, and pay healthcare workers. However, a high GDP does not automatically mean the health sector is well-funded. Policy choices determine whether national wealth actually translates into universal health coverage, functional primary healthcare centers, and adequate nurse-to-patient ratios.

headings.title: Limitations of GDP and GNP in Measuring Population Health
headings.content:
- **Quality of life ignored**: Neither GDP nor GNP measures happiness, stress levels, or actual health outcomes like infant mortality.
- **Inequality blindness**: An economy can show rising GDP while the majority of citizens cannot afford basic healthcare.
- **Environmental factors**: Depleting natural resources or industrial pollution that causes respiratory illnesses can actually increase GDP through medical treatment costs.
- **Unpaid labor**: Caregiving provided by family members at home is completely omitted from economic output calculations.
